Notes to myself, Sangeeta, Sunday.
Visited Gopika at her college hostel with a tiffin of her favourite avial. She hugged me at the gate, 'Bua, you came!', and asked about everyone except her father. When I mentioned that my brother Mohan had asked whether she's eating properly, she went still and said, 'He asked?' I said yes, and nothing more.
Thursday I'd sat with Mohan on his verandah. He asked, pretending not to care, if she still wears the silver anklets. I told him she does. He looked at his hands for a long time.
I'm not going to carry arguments or push either of them to call. Just small true things, both ways, until one of them is ready.
Next: take Gopika's exam timetable when I visit Mohan.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta take to Gopika at the hostel?
qa.a: A tiffin of her favourite avial.

qa.q: What does Gopika's 'He asked?' suggest she feels about her father?
qa.a: It suggests she still cares and is surprised he thinks of her; under the distance she may be longing for some sign from him.

qa.q: Why is Sangeeta's choice not to push either side wise at this stage?
qa.a: Both are proud and hurt, so pressure could make them defend their positions; small true messages let softness travel without anyone losing face.

qa.q: What might Mohan be feeling as he looks at his hands after hearing about the anklets?
qa.a: He likely feels a rush of missing his daughter and sadness at the distance, even while pretending not to care.

grounding: An aunt carries small, true signs of missing each other between her estranged niece and brother, without pushing either to call.

passage:
12 October
Aunt Salma came by the flat again with lemon cake. She never brings up Mum directly, which is why I let her in.
Today, while I was making tea, she said lightly, 'Your mum kept your drawing of the ferry on the fridge. Still there.' Then she talked about the bus strike and her neighbour's cat.
I noticed she didn't ask me to call. She didn't say Mum was sorry either, which I'd have known was a lie. Just that one small thing, then back to the cat.
I think she does the same at Mum's. Maybe she tells her I still drink from the blue mug.
I'm not calling. Not yet. But I keep thinking about that fridge.
- Elizabeth

qa.q: What did Aunt Salma bring to the flat?
qa.a: She brought lemon cake.

qa.q: Why does Elizabeth keep thinking about the fridge?
qa.a: The drawing still on Mum's fridge hints that Mum misses Elizabeth, and that small sign has stirred hope and longing despite the distance.

qa.q: What makes Aunt Salma's way of carrying messages work?
qa.a: She shares one small true detail and then changes the subject, never pushing or inventing apologies, so Elizabeth's pride isn't threatened and trust stays intact.

qa.q: What might Mum feel if Aunt Salma tells her about the blue mug?
qa.a: She would probably feel a soft ache and some hope, learning that Elizabeth still keeps small links to home.

grounding: A young person's diary notices an aunt passing a gentle sign of missing between estranged relatives without pressing for contact.

Sushila Bua visited her brother Jeevan's farm every Tuesday with a tiffin of karela. This Tuesday she sat on the charpai and watched him mend the pump in silence.
"Vaibhav called me," she said at last. "From Pune. He asked if your knee still hurts."
Jeevan's hands stopped.
"I'm not telling you to call him," she said. "I'm only telling you he asked."
On Friday she took the bus to Pune and met Vaibhav at a tea stall. "Your father stopped working when I said your name," she told him. "That's all I know. Do what feels right."
Vaibhav looked down at his cup for a long time.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav ask Sushila Bua about?
qa.a: Whether his father's knee still hurts.

qa.q: What was Sushila Bua feeling when she said "I'm only telling you he asked"?
qa.a: She seems careful and caring, wanting to carry softness between them without pushing either one's pride.

qa.q: Why is Sushila Bua a good go-between at this stage?
qa.a: She carries only small true signs of care to each side and leaves the choice to them, so neither feels trapped.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav be experiencing as he looks at his cup?
qa.a: He is probably moved and unsure, hearing that his father stopped working at his name.

grounding: Shows an aunt carrying small signs of missing each other between a father and son, without pushing either.

Astrid met her nephew for coffee near his university in Uppsala. Rafael talked about his flat, his course, his new bike. Not his father.
When the cups were empty, Astrid said, "Your dad has kept your old skis waxed. Every winter."
Rafael gave a short laugh. "He said I wasn't welcome."
"He did say that. He also asked me last month what size boots you wear now."
Rafael stared out at the snow. Astrid didn't say anything more. She had promised herself: tell each of them one true thing, then step back.
That night she phoned her brother. "Rafael asked if you still ski on Sundays," she said. "I told him yes."

qa.q: Where did Astrid meet Rafael?
qa.a: Near his university in Uppsala.

qa.q: Why did Astrid stop talking after mentioning the boots?
qa.a: She felt a careful kind of caring, wanting to share one true thing without pushing Rafael, as she had promised herself.

qa.q: What makes Astrid's approach useful at this stage?
qa.a: She tells each side one true sign of care and then steps back, so neither's pride is attacked.

qa.q: What is Rafael experiencing as he stares at the snow?
qa.a: He seems torn, hurt by being told he wasn't welcome but moved to hear his father still thinks of him.

grounding: Shows an aunt quietly telling a nephew and his father that each still thinks of the other, without pushing either.

The visitors' room at Eshaan's college hostel was empty except for a ceiling fan and Vidya Bua with a steel box of laddoos. "Your father sends nothing," she said, before he could ask. "But he asked me twice in one week whether you're eating properly."
Eshaan looked at the floor. "He said that?"
"Twice." She didn't say more. She didn't say, "Call him." She just watched his jaw soften and then harden again.
That Sunday, at her brother's house, Vidya Bua mentioned over tea that Eshaan still kept the old watch his father had given him on his hostel desk. Her brother put down his cup and went quiet. Vidya Bua said nothing further. She had carried one small warm thing each way; what they did with it was theirs to decide.

qa.q: What did Eshaan's father ask Vidya Bua twice in one week?
qa.a: Whether Eshaan is eating properly.

qa.q: Why does Vidya Bua not tell Eshaan to call his father?
qa.a: She seems caring but careful, feeling that pushing would wound their pride, so she trusts them to decide.

qa.q: Why does a go-between like Vidya Bua help at this stage?
qa.a: She carries a soft, true message each way, that each still cares, when direct contact feels too risky for both prides.

qa.q: What is it like for Eshaan to hear that his father asked about him twice?
qa.a: Eshaan is moved and unsettled, his jaw softening and hardening as longing and old hurt pull against each other.

grounding: Shows an aunt quietly telling a son and his father that the other still cares, without pushing either, opening a door neither could open alone.
